nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the imagist theory and the classical revolt
literary_identity: Poet, critic and philosopher; the founder of Imagism and the theorist of the classical reaction against Romanticism.
biography: Born Thomas Ernest Hulme at Endon, Staffordshire, on 16 September 1883; he studied at Cambridge and London, founded the Poets' Club in 1908, and published the five poems and the criticism that made him the theoretical founder of Imagism and of the classical revival. He served in the Royal Marine Artillery and was killed by a shell at Nieuport on 28 September 1917. Speculations appeared in 1924.
literary_profile: T. E. Hulme was the founder of Imagism and the theorist of the classical reaction against Romanticism: his five poems and his criticism made him the intellectual founder of the modern movement in English poetry, and Speculations is the central document of the classical revival that shaped Eliot, Pound and the New Criticism.
stylistic_characteristics: The image as the unit of poetry; the free verse of the few poems; the critical essay of the classical reaction; the polemic against Romanticism; the plain, hard, exact argument.
intellectual_concerns: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist; mass society, the crowd, and the individual talent; religion, doubt, and the post-war faith; the absurd, the void.
historical_significance: T. E. Hulme was the founder of Imagism and the theorist of the classical reaction against Romanticism: his five poems and his criticism made him the intellectual founder of the modern movement in English poetry, and Speculations is the central document of the classical revival.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Depression novel and the California valley
literary_identity: Novelist; the great American novelist of the Depression and the Nobel laureate of 1962.
biography: Born John Ernst Steinbeck Jr in Salinas, California, on 27 February 1902; he worked as a labourer, fruit picker and journalist, and made his name with Tortilla Flat (1935). Of Mice and Men (1937), The Grapes of Wrath (1939), Cannery Row (1945) and East of Eden (1952) followed; he was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1962 and died in New York on 20 December 1968.
literary_profile: Steinbeck was the great American novelist of the Depression and the Nobel laureate of 1962: The Grapes of Wrath is the central American novel of the 1930s and Of Mice and Men one of the most performed plays and novels in the language, and his California valley gave American fiction a permanent landscape.
stylistic_characteristics: The documentary detail of the migrant road; the flat, plain, biblical prose; the dialogue of the dispossessed; the intercalary chapter and the wide social view; the compassion without sentimentality.
intellectual_concerns: The Depression, unemployment, and the hunger march; the closing of the American frontier; money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination; class, the servant problem, and the new democracy.
historical_significance: Steinbeck was the great American novelist of the Depression and the Nobel laureate of 1962: The Grapes of Wrath is the central American novel of the 1930s, Of Mice and Men one of the most performed works in the language, and his California valley gave American fiction a permanent landscape.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the prairie novel and the pioneer memory
literary_identity: Novelist; the great American novelist of the pioneer West and the finest American prose stylist of the period.
biography: Born Wilella Sibert Cather at Winchester, Virginia, on 7 December 1873; her family moved to Nebraska in 1883, and she worked as a journalist and teacher before O Pioneers! (1913) made her name. My Antonia (1918), A Lost Lady (1923), The Professor's House (1925) and Death Comes for the Archbishop (1927) followed. She died in New York on 24 April 1947.
literary_profile: Willa Cather was the great American novelist of the pioneer West and the finest American prose stylist of the period: O Pioneers! and My Antonia created the prairie novel, Death Comes for the Archbishop is one of the great American novels of the century, and her prose gave American fiction its most classical style.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain, exact, unhurried sentence; the landscape as the determining force; the pioneer and the immigrant; the elegy for the vanished frontier; the refusal of plot in favour of the remembered image.
intellectual_concerns: The closing of the American frontier; the American wilderness and the myth of the forest; regional identity and the American sectional character; innocence, experience, and the lost American Eden.
historical_significance: Willa Cather was the great American novelist of the pioneer West and the finest American prose stylist of the period: O Pioneers! and My Antonia created the prairie novel, and Death Comes for the Archbishop is one of the great American novels of the century.

literary_identity: Novelist; the first American to win the Nobel Prize for Literature, and the great satirist of the American small town and the business culture.
biography: Born Harry Sinclair Lewis in Sauk Centre, Minnesota, on 7 February 1885; he worked as a journalist and editor, and made his name with Main Street (1920). Babbitt (1922), Arrowsmith (1925), Elmer Gantry (1927) and It Can't Happen Here (1935) followed; he was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1930 and died in Rome on 10 January 1951.
literary_profile: Sinclair Lewis was the first American to win the Nobel Prize for Literature and the great satirist of the American small town: Main Street and Babbitt created the American novel of the provincial city, and Elmer Gantry and It Can't Happen Here extended the satire to religion and to fascism.
stylistic_characteristics: The documentary accumulation of detail; the satirical caricature with a name that becomes a type; the dialogue of the booster and the salesman; the wide social panorama; the plain, energetic, journalistic prose.
intellectual_concerns: The American city, the machine, and the moneyed metropolis; regional identity and the American sectional character; democracy, individualism, and the American experiment; industrial wealth, accumulation, and the gospel of accumulation.

literary_identity: Playwright; the founder of the modern American theatre and the Nobel laureate of 1936.
biography: Born Eugene Gladstone O'Neill in a Broadway hotel in New York on 16 October 1888, the son of the actor James O'Neill; he went to sea, worked as a reporter, and made his name with Beyond the Horizon (1920, Pulitzer Prize). The Emperor Jones (1920), Anna Christie (1921), Desire Under the Elms (1924), Strange Interlude (1928), Mourning Becomes Electra (1931) and Long Day's Journey into Night (written 1940) followed. He died in Boston on 27 November 1953.
literary_profile: Eugene O'Neill founded the modern American theatre and was the first American playwright to win the Nobel Prize: his experimental plays brought expressionism, psychoanalysis and the classical tragedy into the American theatre, and he is the central figure of American drama in the century.
stylistic_characteristics: The expressionist set and the mask; the long monologue and the aside spoken to the audience; the dialect of the sailor and the farmer; the classical tragedy in a New England house; the plain, insistent, repetitive speech of obsession.
intellectual_concerns: Sexuality, the new psychology; class, the servant problem, and the new democracy; the American city, the machine, and the moneyed metropolis; the body, illness, and the sanatorium.
historical_significance: Eugene O'Neill founded the modern American theatre and was the first American playwright to win the Nobel Prize: his experimental plays brought expressionism, psychoanalysis and classical tragedy into the American theatre, and he is the central figure of American drama in the century.

literary_identity: Novelist and playwright; the only writer to win Pulitzer Prizes for both fiction and drama, and the author of Our Town and The Bridge of San Luis Rey.
biography: Born Thornton Niven Wilder in Madison, Wisconsin, on 17 April 1897; his family lived in China, and he taught at Chicago and Harvard. The Bridge of San Luis Rey (1927) won the Pulitzer Prize, and Our Town (1938) and The Skin of Our Teeth (1942) made him the central American playwright of the period. He died in Hamden, Connecticut, on 7 December 1975.
literary_profile: Thornton Wilder was the only writer to win Pulitzer Prizes for both fiction and drama: Our Town created the modern American theatre of the bare stage and The Bridge of San Luis Rey one of the great American novels of the century, and his humanism shaped the American stage for a generation.
stylistic_characteristics: The bare stage and the Stage Manager; the plain, direct address to the audience; the ordinary life of the small town; the philosophical frame; the refusal of spectacle.
intellectual_concerns: Death, the soul, and the afterlife; the suburb, the villa, and the new domesticity; religion, doubt, and the post-war faith; the absurd, the void.
historical_significance: Thornton Wilder was the only writer to win Pulitzer Prizes for both fiction and drama: Our Town created the modern American theatre of the bare stage, and The Bridge of San Luis Rey is one of the great American novels of the century.

biography: Born Nathan Weinstein in New York on 17 October 1903; he changed his name, worked in a hotel and for a newspaper, and published The Dream Life of Balso Snell (1931), Miss Lonelyhearts (1933) and A Cool Million (1934). The Day of the Locust (1939) followed; he died in a car crash in California on 22 December 1940.

stylistic_characteristics: The grotesque image and the surreal scene; the short novel of the obsessive; the black comedy without consolation; the Hollywood crowd and the mob; the flat, hard, exact prose.

birthplace: St Mary's County, Maryland, United States
literary_identity: Writer of detective fiction; the founder of the hard-boiled school and the author of The Maltese Falcon.
biography: Born Samuel Dashiell Hammett in St Mary's County, Maryland, on 27 May 1894; he worked as a Pinkerton detective from 1915 to 1922, and drew on the experience for Red Harvest (1929), The Dain Curse (1929), The Maltese Falcon (1930), The Glass Key (1931) and The Thin Man (1934). He was blacklisted and imprisoned in the 1950s and died in New York on 10 January 1961.
literary_profile: Dashiell Hammett founded the hard-boiled detective novel and is the central figure of American crime fiction: Red Harvest, The Maltese Falcon and The Thin Man created the private eye, the corrupt city and the dialogue that made the American crime novel a serious literary form.
stylistic_characteristics: The first-person narration of the private eye; the clipped, laconic dialogue; the corrupt city and the double cross; the violence sudden and unexplained; the moral code of the outsider.
intellectual_concerns: The American city, the machine, and the moneyed metropolis; money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination; mass society, the crowd, and the individual talent; the absurd, the void.
historical_significance: Dashiell Hammett founded the hard-boiled detective novel and is the central figure of American crime fiction: Red Harvest, The Maltese Falcon and The Thin Man created the private eye and the corrupt city, and made the American crime novel a serious literary form.
